name: Rosehip oil

lead: Rosehip oil is pressed from the seeds of wild roses and is used to moisturize skin, with the aim of softening the look of scars, stretch marks and uneven tone.

The oil contains linoleic, linolenic and oleic fatty acids plus tocopherols, carotenoids and phenolic compounds, and Wikipedia attributes proposed anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects to this content. A laboratory wound-healing study reported accelerated healing via macrophage changes, and some research on inflammatory skin conditions has promising findings. No human trial of rosehip oil specifically for scars was identified.

paras: People apply a few drops to the face or scar, usually as a daily step in a routine, often at night, and use it for weeks to months. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient and as a standalone oil.
The sources reviewed give no safety data. As with any plant oil, a patch test is a common precaution.

angle.text: Rosehip oil is a fatty-acid-rich seed oil applied to moisturize skin and soften the look of scars and stretch marks. Lab and small studies exist, and clear human scar trials were not found.

lead: Rosehip oil, also called rose hip seed oil, is a vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of wild roses, most commonly Rosa rubiginosa from the southern Andes or Rosa canina from Europe and western Asia [1]. People apply it to the skin as a facial or body oil, hoping to make scars, stretch marks, uneven tone and dry or dull skin look smoother and healthier.

Proponents point to its mix of essential fatty acids (linoleic and linolenic), antioxidants such as tocopherols and carotenoids, and provitamin A, which they associate with skin repair and softness [1]. Lifting and bodybuilding forums mention it mainly for stretch marks that appear with rapid muscle or weight gain [2][3].

Published work includes compositional and authenticity analyses, laboratory and animal wound-healing studies, formulation studies in which the oil is one ingredient among several, and a few small human studies of multi-ingredient or branded rosehip products, including one in radiotherapy skin care.[4][5][6][7] No trial testing rosehip oil alone for scars or stretch marks in people has been published.
infobox: Linoleic, linolenic and oleic acids; tocopherols; carotenoids

paras: The oil is extracted from the seeds inside rose hips, the fruit of the rose plant. Wikipedia describes rose seed oil as a vegetable seed oil and notes that rose fruits have a long place in folk medicine.[1] Rose hips themselves are eaten in teas, jams, soups and drinks, and Wikipedia's rose hip page notes wild hips are rich in vitamin C, carotenoids and other compounds, though that describes the fruit rather than the seed oil.[8]

Commercial rosehip oil is sold cold-pressed or refined, alone or as an ingredient in serums, balms and creams. Analytical papers on mid-infrared and Raman spectroscopy describe methods for detecting adulteration of the oil, which indicates that product authenticity is a recognized issue.[9][10] The oil is often marketed under the name rosa mosqueta, from Chile and the southern Andes, where Rosa rubiginosa grows wild.[1]

Wikipedia lists linoleic, linolenic and oleic fatty acids, delta- and gamma-tocopherol, carotenoids and phenolic compounds as constituents, and notes that provitamin A, mostly beta-carotene, is present [1]. Spectroscopic methods have been used to characterise the oil and to detect adulteration [9][10].

A 2005 gas chromatography study cited by Wikipedia identified compounds including vitispiran, dodecanoic and hexadecanoic acids and ionone alongside linoleic acid [1]. The oil is reported to contain no vitamin A itself but provitamin A and all-trans retinoic acid, which is one reason it is often compared with retinoid skincare [1].

Rosehip oil is applied to skin as a cosmetic oil, usually a few drops massaged into the face, scars or stretch marks, or blended into other products. People use it hoping to improve the look of scars, stretch marks, dryness, dullness and uneven tone. It also appears as an ingredient in nanoemulsion and nanocapsule formulations, for example with kojic dipalmitate for melasma and with isotretinoin and quercetin in a laboratory acne-related formulation; these are formulation studies rather than tests of the oil alone.[11][12]

Wikipedia reports that researchers tested topical rose hip seed oil with oral fat-soluble vitamins on inflammatory skin conditions such as eczema, with promising findings, though it flags the source as possibly unreliable.[1] A 2019 Planta Medica study reported that the oil promoted excisional wound healing in an animal model by accelerating macrophage phenotypic transition.[13]

A 2024 review of rosehip extract and wound healing summarizes preclinical and clinical findings on the fruit and its extracts, which are broader than the seed oil.[4] Cosmetic-science reviews of nanocarrier formulations treat rosehip oil as one of several plant oils used to deliver active ingredients.[14]
No trial of rosehip oil alone for scars in humans has been published. Several small human studies have used rosehip oil within defined products.

A 2013 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in pregnant women tested a cream containing hydroxyprolisilane C, rosehip oil, Centella asiatica triterpenes and vitamin E against a plain cream. Overall incidence of new stretch marks was 33.3% in controls and 37.6% in the treated group, not significantly different; however, the severity of previous stretch marks increased in the control group but not in the treated group, and among women who developed new marks the treated group showed a smaller increase in severity.[7]

A 2016 Spanish exploratory, controlled, open study of 28 head-and-neck cancer patients receiving intensity-modulated radiotherapy applied a rosehip oil product twice daily and compared them with 34 earlier patients who had used other skin products; the groups were comparable, and the report examined the number of treatments needed and the grade of radiation skin reaction.[5]

A 2022 randomized, double-blind trial of 40 people with intertrigo compared an adsorbent lotion containing rosehip oil among other ingredients with 1% hydrocortisone cream over two weeks and reported higher reduction in itching with the lotion.[6]

Rosehip oil is mentioned in physique-focused communities chiefly for stretch marks that appear with rapid muscle gain. One 2013 T Nation poster suggests rosehip oil for stretch marks that come from growing too fast for the skin to keep up, while others recommend it with Bio-Oil and cocoa butter.[3][2] A 2012 forum reply describes it as useful on scar tissue and on skin exposed to the elements.[15]

lore.intro: On T Nation, rosehip oil shows up in short replies to stretch-mark threads alongside Bio-Oil and cocoa butter, and in a 2012 thread where a poster calls it a strong skin protector [2][3][15].
